events.text: Day 1 begins.

We have no evidence yet, so I’d avoid treating an early accusation as more than a starting point. With five votes needed to eliminate today, it’s worth hearing people’s reasoning and remembering that votes will be public afterward. I’d also avoid pressuring anyone to reveal a role.

I agree with Lucia that we should hear everyone's reasoning today. Since votes are public and will remain available later, I think it's worth being thoughtful about what we say now. I don't have any strong reads yet on Day 1, but I'd like to hear from more people before we start forming opinions. If anyone has a gut feeling or observation from the opening, I'm listening.

So far we've heard two cautious, reasonable openings - Lucia and Priya both emphasized listening before accusing. That's a good sign, but it also means we've barely scratched the surface with five players still silent. On Day 1 with no real information, I think the most valuable thing we can do is get everyone talking so we can compare tone and reasoning when we have more to work with later. I'd encourage people who haven't spoken yet to share whatever gut read or observation they have, even if it's just a feeling. Silence isn't suspicious yet, but it also doesn't help us.

Thanks, Leo. I agree that the opening has been cautious but not empty: Lucia and Priya set a sensible tone, and Leo’s push for more voices is reasonable on Day 1. I don’t have a strong read yet, and I don’t think we should invent one just to have a target. With five votes needed and public voting history, the useful thing now is to hear from the players who haven’t spoken, compare how specific people are with their reasoning, and avoid pressuring role reveals this early. I’m not blaming anyone from the opening alone.

Noah's point about not inventing a read just to have a target is the right frame for us right now, and I want to add one narrow thing to it: the absence of a target today isn't a waste of a day, it may be the cheapest day we get. The first vote that actually eliminates someone also permanently removes a player from every future night, so a rushed Day 1 elimination is a decision we only get to make once and with no data behind it. Five votes needed also means a single accusation carries almost no weight; the votes are public, so what matters today is which reasoning we find ourselves repeating, not who we point at first.

For my own part, I have no read on anyone. I've watched the four openings and they are consistent with each other: cautious, non-accusatory, and explicitly declining to pressure role claims. I'm not going to treat that consistency as evidence of innocence either, since cautious Day 1 behavior is what a good player and a lucky player both produce. What I will do is pay attention over the next few days to whether someone's claims about what they observed become more specific as time goes on, or stay vague, and whether anyone starts pushing very hard for a specific target without adding new information to justify it. That pressure-without-evidence pattern would tell me more than anything said today.

Sam, you haven't spoken yet, so let me ask you one specific question rather than a general one: in your view, did anything about the order or timing of the early speakers look deliberate to you — anyone pausing unusually long, or jumping in right after another player's point in a way that felt rehearsed? I'm asking because I can't evaluate that from inside my own turn, and it's the only concrete observation anyone might have that the rest of us can't generate ourselves.

Theo, to answer your question directly: I can't see any timing or pacing in the record. We only have the text of each message, with no timestamps or pauses, so I can't say whether anyone's order looked deliberate. The only pattern I can point to is that the first four openings all urged caution and avoided role pressure. That fits a town player and a mafia player trying to blend in equally well, so it doesn't separate anyone yet. I agree with you that the useful signal is whether claims become more specific over the next few days, or whether someone pushes hard for a target without adding information. I have no read on anyone today, and I'm not going to pick a target just to move the day along. I'll be looking for concrete observations in the next discussion.

Sam is right that we can’t infer pauses or timing from this record. I also think we should be careful about treating an abstention as cost-free: it avoids an uninformed elimination, but mafia still get a night kill. On the other hand, forcing a vote without a reason can eliminate a town player. I don’t have a defensible suspect yet, and I’ll weigh both risks when voting.

I appreciate Omar introducing some nuance to the discussion. While Theo is right that a reckless elimination permanently costs town a member with very little data, Omar makes the critical counterpoint: doing nothing gives the mafia a completely uncontested night kill and deprives town of an informative voting record to look back on tomorrow.

Cautious play on Day 1 is natural for both town and mafia, which is why the early agreement didn't tell us much. The true value of Day 1 isn't necessarily finding mafia right out of the gate—which is nearly impossible without claims or results—but forcing players onto the public record so that later claims, shifts in tone, or bandwagoning can be cross-checked against actual commitments.

I don't have a confident suspect yet, and I agree we shouldn't fabricate an accusation out of thin air. However, we should be realistic about the trade-off Omar highlighted before automatically assuming a no-elimination day is harmless.

Kenji's framing is the right one for where we are, and I want to sharpen the concrete part of it.

Every opening we've heard so far has been cautious and non-accusatory: Lucia, Priya, Leo, Noah, Sam, Omar, Kenji. I agree that this consistency is uninformative — it's the baseline for both sides, and treating it as evidence either way would be a mistake. So I won't claim anyone is guilty and I won't vote for a name today unless a claim is made that can be checked.

But I also accept Omar's counterpoint more strongly than the general agreement so far has. A no-elimination day is not free: it hands the mafia a clean night kill, and it hands them a night where our non-actions produce no information about anyone. The thing we get for free on Day 1 is not certainty, it's a public baseline. After today, every player's first statements are fixed, and tomorrow we can compare what they said against what they do. That comparison is only available if we actually record something today.

So here's my practical position: I'll vote today, but only for a target whose claim is internally inconsistent with what they said in their own opening. Nobody has made such a claim yet, so my vote today will likely be an abstention or a low-confidence choice, and I'd rather say that plainly than manufacture a reason. What I'd like to avoid is a day where five or six of us each vote for a different name out of pure momentum — that creates noise, and noise gets laundered into consensus tomorrow.

The specific thing I said earlier still stands as my main watch item: claims that become more specific over time without new information, and pressure for a target that isn't backed by new information. Both are checkable against this record, and I'll be checking.

Arjun, you haven't spoken yet. Rather than ask a general "what do you think," I'll ask one narrow question: when you read the seven openings, did any single player's statements contain a specific factual claim about the game state — something checkable like who they saw or what they heard — and if so, whose was it and did it look invented rather than observed? If there was no such claim anywhere, say so; that itself tells us the Day 1 record has no leverage in it, and it's more useful to me than a general opinion.

Theo, to answer your question directly: no. I went back over the seven openings, and not one of them contains a specific factual claim about the game state — nothing checkable about who they saw, what they heard, or anything observable. Everyone offered general reasoning about caution, abstention costs, and voting mechanics, which is fair enough on Day 1, but there is nothing in this record that can be tested against anything. So by your own standard, the Day 1 record as it stands has no leverage in it.

I'll say what I take from that. First, I agree with the consensus here that nobody should be eliminated today on the basis of what's been said, because there's literally nothing in anyone's opening that separates town from mafia. The only concrete thing anyone has offered is the observation that we can't see timing or pacing, which Sam pointed out.

Second, on Omar's trade-off point: I think he's right that a no-elimination day isn't free, but I'd weight it the other way. With nine players alive and five votes needed for a unique leader, the chance that today's vote lands on a mafia player by accident is low, while the chance it lands on a town player is high. Losing one town player to a coin-flip vote plus one to the night kill puts us in a worse hole than losing one to the night kill alone. I'd rather bank the baseline this discussion has created and let tomorrow's votes happen with one night's worth of information behind them.

Third, on Theo's watch item about claims becoming more specific over time without new information: I'll be watching for that too, and I'd add one related thing — tomorrow, after the night result, the useful question for each player will be whether their read on anyone actually incorporates the new information or just restates their Day 1 position. Someone whose reasoning doesn't move at all after events have moved is either very confident or not reasoning from the events at all. That's the first checkable thing we'll have.

For my own part, I have no read on anyone and I'm not going to manufacture one. My vote today will most likely be an abstention, unless something checkable surfaces before voting closes.

Arjun's answer settles my second question: the Day 1 record contains no checkable factual claims, so by my own standard there is no leverage in it and no basis for an accusation today. I'm not going to manufacture one, and I'm saying that as a position, not as a hedge.

Where I land, stated plainly: I expect to abstain today. Not because abstention is free — I've made that point twice and I still hold it, because a no-elimination day hands the mafia an uncontested night kill and costs town a member permanently, and a vote on no information risks costing us a town member for nothing. But a coin-flip elimination with nine players alive and five votes needed to move anyone is a worse bet than one clean night loss. I'll take the night loss and keep the baseline.

Two things I want on the record for tomorrow, since these are the only checkable things we'll have:

First, Arjun's addition is the sharpest test available: after the night result, a player's read either incorporates the new information or merely restates their Day 1 position. Repetition across a changed board is a signal, and it cuts toward whoever's read was loudest and least responsive. Note that this is a test for our own reasoning too — including mine. If the night changes nothing for me, I should ask why.

Second, my earlier watch item stands unchanged: claims that get more specific without new information, and pressure for a target not backed by new information. On Day 1 that pressure has been absent from everyone, which I count as genuinely uninformative rather than as exculpatory.

One more thing about my own behavior tonight, for transparency and for my own planning: I will protect someone tonight, and I'm not going to announce who, because saying it out loud would defeat the purpose and would give the other side information about my pattern. I'd rather the public record of my protection choices be invisible than predictable.

Omar, one specific question on your point about the cost of abstention, because you framed it most carefully: how would you distinguish, on tomorrow's record, between a town player whose reasoning genuinely doesn't move because there was nothing to reason about, and a mafia player who is deliberately keeping their reasoning flat to avoid a checkable commitment? I'd rather have your answer to that than a general read, and it will help me calibrate what I'm looking for.

Theo, I don’t think a flat read alone distinguishes town from mafia. A night death may not reveal much, especially since roles aren’t revealed on death. I’d look instead at whether someone explains what the result does and doesn’t change, engages with alternatives, and makes consistent commitments when there is something concrete to evaluate. None of that is proof by itself.

Your statement that you’ll protect someone tonight sounds like a doctor claim. That is significant, but I can’t verify it. I don’t think anyone should disclose their own role in response, and I won’t treat the claim alone as proof of either alignment. We should remember it when interpreting what happens next.

I still see costs on both sides of abstaining. I have no defensible suspect at present, so I’m not going to force a name merely to produce a vote.

Omar’s distinction makes sense: a night result may not give us enough to change a read, particularly without role reveals. Explanations and responses to alternatives matter more than a change in position by itself.

Theo’s apparent doctor claim is important, but unverified. I agree that nobody should feel pressured to respond with a role claim. For today, I don’t have a defensible target and expect to abstain.

I agree with Omar and Arjun that nothing in the Day 1 openings is checkable yet, so I won't name anyone. Theo's statement that he will protect someone tonight is a role-type claim. I can't verify it, and I won't treat it as proof either way. I'd like to see whether it stays consistent with Theo's later statements and whether the night result fits it. For my own vote today, I expect to abstain unless a checkable claim appears before voting closes. If the night produces a death, I'll look at who explains what that result changes and who sticks to a position without engaging the new information.

Following up on my earlier answer to Theo, and on the exchange since: I still have no read on anyone, and nothing said in the last few turns has changed that.

But I want to flag one consequence of Theo's protection statement that I think is worth having on the record now, because it affects how we interpret tomorrow night. Theo has publicly committed to protecting someone. If he is genuine, the mafia now have a reason to consider him a high-value target — and Theo himself acknowledged the cost of announcing it. That creates a checkable pattern: if Theo is attacked tonight and survives, either his claim was real or the mafia avoided him for their own reasons. If someone else dies while Theo lives, the claim remains unverified but unfalsified. I agree with Omar that the claim alone proves nothing, and I agree with Sam and Lucia that nobody should feel pressured to respond with a role claim of their own. What I'd add is that we shouldn't over-read a quiet night either way, since a night with no death has multiple explanations and we won't be able to separate them.

On the vote itself: I said I'd likely abstain, and that stands. Five votes are needed to eliminate, the Day 1 record contains nothing checkable, and I'd rather bank the baseline than force an elimination that most likely costs town a member. The one thing that would move me is a specific, checkable claim surfacing before voting closes — not a general position, but something we can test against tomorrow's result.

Lastly, on Theo's question to Omar about flat reasoning: I thought Omar's answer was right. The test isn't whether a read changes, it's whether a player's reasoning engages with what actually happened. I'll be applying that standard to myself too.

Theo's remark about protecting someone tonight definitely caught my attention. An unforced doctor soft-claim on Day 1 is unusual and naturally invites mafia scrutiny, but as Omar and others have rightly pointed out, there is no way to verify it today, and under no circumstances should anyone else claim or contest it. We simply have to log it for future reference and see how the game develops.

Regarding the Day 1 vote: when I reinforced Omar's point earlier about the costs of abstaining, it was to ensure we weighed the trade-offs rather than assuming a skipped vote is completely harmless. That said, looking at where the discussion has landed, there are genuinely no checkable claims or contradictions on the board. Forcing a blind elimination with nine alive carries a high probability of hitting a town player, which compounded with a night kill would put us in a much deeper hole. Given the lack of actionable data, I agree with the consensus that abstaining is the most sensible play today.

I have no target to name right now, and unless something unexpected surfaces before the vote, I intend to abstain.

Thanks, everyone. I've read the openings and agree with the consensus that nothing checkable has surfaced yet, so I won't name anyone today. Theo's protection statement is unverified, and I won't treat it as proof either way, but I'll keep it on the record and check it against tonight's result. Omar and Arjun both pointed to the test I care about most: whether people's reasoning engages with what actually happened overnight, not whether their position changes for its own sake. I'll be looking for that from everyone, including myself. My vote today will be an abstention unless a specific, checkable claim appears before voting closes.

I've been following this discussion and I want to note where we've landed: eight of us have now publicly said we expect to abstain, and the only substantive new information since the openings is Theo's statement that he'll protect someone tonight — an unforced doctor-type soft-claim that nobody has contested or copied, which I agree we should log and not respond to with role reveals of our own.

What I want to put on the record before we close discussion is a mild observation about the shape of this conversation. The consensus toward abstention arrived quickly and almost nobody has dissented from it. That may be the right call — the Day 1 record genuinely contains nothing checkable, and I said myself earlier that silence and generic caution don't help us — but unanimous agreement with no pushback is worth noting, because it means we haven't stress-tested the position at all. If even one person genuinely thinks we should force a vote today, I'd rather hear that argument now than discover tomorrow that everyone privately had reservations.

The one player whose reasoning I'd like to hear more from is Noah, since he raised the point about not inventing a read just to have a target early on, and that framing has shaped much of the discussion since. Noah — you were the first to articulate the 'no manufactured target' position before Theo, Omar, and the rest built on it. Now that we've had a full discussion and still have zero checkable claims, does the speed and unanimity of this consensus concern you at all, or do you see it as exactly the correct outcome given what's on the table? I'm asking because your early framing set the tone and I'd like your own read on where it led us, not just whether you're abstaining.

Leo, directly: the unanimity is worth noting, but it doesn't move me toward suspicion. My early point was not that silence is suspicious; it was that we shouldn't invent a target. Given nine alive, five votes needed, and no checkable claim, abstention is the coherent outcome rather than a suspicious bandwagon. The speed matters only if someone is hiding a real disagreement; I'd rather hear that now than later. I don't have one, and I won't manufacture one.

Theo's protection statement is the one substantive event. I agree it should be logged, not treated as proof; nobody should claim or contest a role because of it. Tomorrow the useful test is whether people's reasoning actually incorporates the night result — whether they explain what changed and what didn't — not whether their position changes for appearance. I'll apply that to myself too. Today I expect to abstain unless a specific checkable claim appears.

I want to note something about the trajectory of this discussion. Leo asked whether the speed and unanimity of the abstention consensus should concern us, and I think that's the right question to keep alive even as we head into voting.

On the merits, I agree with where we've landed: the Day 1 record contains nothing checkable, five votes are needed to eliminate, and a blind elimination with nine alive most likely costs town a member. I expect to abstain unless something checkable appears before voting closes.

But I want to commit us to two things now, before tonight's result shapes how we think:

First, one night of data constrains very little with nine players and two mafia. Whether someone dies or nobody dies, we should resist the urge to anchor hard on that single data point. Tomorrow's analysis should engage with what the result does and doesn't tell us, not treat it as a verdict.

Second, Theo's protection statement is the only substantive claim on the record. I agree it should be logged, not responded to with role claims, and not treated as proof either way. What I'll be checking is whether Theo's reasoning and behavior tomorrow are consistent with having a protective role — not just whether he repeats the claim, but whether the substance of his play fits it.

I'd rather say these now than discover tomorrow that we've all quietly over-read or under-read the same event.

I've said my piece on the trajectory and my commitments for tomorrow, so I don't have much to add beyond what's already on the record. The one thing I'll add is that Leo's unanimity point deserves a genuine answer rather than just agreement, and Noah gave one — the distinction between refusing to manufacture a target and refusing to engage at all is real, and I think the discussion has engaged rather than merely defaulted. That said, Priya's and Omar's points about the cost of abstention remain valid counterweights, and if someone has been silently holding a different view, the window to say so is now, before we vote. Otherwise I'm content to let the vote reflect where we've landed: abstention unless something checkable surfaces, with tonight's result and everyone's response to it as the first real test.

I want to close where the discussion has landed, because I think it's the right place: eight of us have now said we expect to abstain, the ninth — Theo — has said he expects to abstain unless a checkable claim appears. Nobody has offered a competing position, and Priya's point that the window to dissent is now is well taken. I'll say clearly that I have no hidden reservation — abstention is my actual read, not a hedge.

The two things I want on the record going into tonight are the ones others have already committed to: Theo's protection statement is logged, unverified, and nobody should respond with role claims; and tomorrow's first real test is whether each player's reasoning engages with the night result rather than restating a Day 1 position. I'll hold myself to that standard too.

If someone has been quietly holding a different view, say it now. Otherwise, I'm content to let the vote reflect unanimity and move to night.

I’m the detective. I investigated Theo last night, and the result is that he is not mafia. That does not verify his doctor-type claim or tell us his exact role, but it does mean he is not on the mafia team. I’m putting that on the record now because it is the first checkable fact we have, and because Theo was the only substantive Day 1 claim. We should not keep treating that claim as entirely unverified when one part of it can now be tested.

Omar’s elimination is the other fact. Roles are not revealed on death, so we cannot infer much from who he was. What matters is whether people’s reasoning actually engages with these two facts — the night kill and the inspection result — instead of restating Day 1 caution. I’ll be watching for anyone who pushes a target without tying it to new information.

I have no accusation yet. I’m not going to name someone just to create momentum. My vote remains open.

I'll apply the test I committed to yesterday: does my reasoning actually engage with what happened overnight, rather than restating Day 1 caution? Two new facts are on the table — Omar's elimination, and Noah's claim of a detective result on Theo — so let me work through both.

First, Noah's claim. It's the first specific factual claim in the game, which is exactly what Theo was asking for on Day 1. I can't verify it, and I agree with the standard we set: nobody should counter-claim or reveal a role under pressure. What I'll note is that if Noah's claim is genuine, it has an immediate consequence — the mafia now know there's an active investigator, which makes Noah a likely target tonight. Whether he's genuine or not, that's a real cost anyone making this claim accepts. I won't treat the result on Theo as proof of Theo's doctor claim, as Noah himself said; it clears him of mafia affiliation, nothing more.

Second, Omar's death. One checkable implication: Theo said publicly he would protect someone last night, and Omar died anyway. So either Theo protected himself, protected someone else who wasn't targeted, or the protection claim doesn't hold. None of those outcomes is incriminating on its own — a doctor protecting himself is perfectly reasonable — but it's the first time one of our claims has collided with a result, so it belongs on the record.

Third, the choice of Omar is worth noticing: he was the player who argued hardest that abstention isn't free. Whether that's why he was targeted, I can't know.

My vote is open. I have no accusation I can defend, and I won't manufacture one.

Continuing to apply the standard I set for myself yesterday. Noah's claim and Omar's death are on the table, so let me engage with both rather than restate caution.

On Noah's claim: I want to be precise about what a 'not mafia' result is actually worth, because it's less than it appears. A claim that someone is cleared costs almost nothing to fabricate. A fake accusation carries risk — it can be tested, contested, and traced back if the accusation falls apart. But a fake clear on a genuinely innocent player is unfalsifiable and buys the claimant instant credibility at zero risk. So the epistemic value of 'Theo is not mafia' depends entirely on whether Noah is a real investigator, and we have no way to check that today. I'm not accusing Noah of anything — the claim may well be genuine — but I want us to log that it can't do the work of exonerating anyone until it's corroborated by something else. Theo's protection claim and Noah's clear pointing at the same person makes them mutually reinforcing only if at least one is true, which is exactly what we can't establish.

On Omar's death: I flagged yesterday that Theo committed publicly to protecting someone, and Omar died anyway. Theo hasn't responded yet to that collision, and I don't want to pile on before he does — there are innocent explanations, self-protection being the most obvious. But it's the first testable commitment we've had, and how Theo addresses it matters more than whether his position changes.

One more structural point about the night. Omar was the player who argued most forcefully that abstention isn't free and that town should pressure for information. Whatever the mafia's reasoning was, killing the loudest advocate for aggressive play is a pattern worth remembering: if it repeats, we learn something about what the mafia fear. If the next elimination is someone quiet and non-committal, we learn something different. I'm not drawing a conclusion from one data point — Priya warned us yesterday against anchoring on a single night — but I'm recording it.

For my own part, my position is where it was: no accusation I can defend, vote open. The things I'll be watching today are whether anyone pushes a target without tying it to the two new facts we have, and whether anyone's stated reasoning incorporates Omar's death at all or just proceeds as if it didn't happen. Yesterday we agreed that a read which doesn't engage with events is the first checkable signal we'd get. The night gave us events. Today is when that test actually runs.

Theo, I want to put the collision to you directly rather than let it sit: yesterday you publicly said you would protect someone, and Omar died. That doesn't make you mafia—my investigation says you are not—but it is the first commitment of yours that a night result can test. Can you address it specifically: did you protect yourself, or if not, does your choice help explain why Omar died? You don't need to name a target if you think that would give mafia information; I'm asking for the reasoning, not a role reveal.

For everyone else: my detective result clears Theo of being mafia and nothing more. I have no second result and no accusation. Arjun's point that a fake 'not mafia' clear is cheap is fair in the abstract, but it cuts both ways: if I were mafia, clearing Theo would be a strange play when he had already soft-claimed doctor and was under scrutiny—I'd be tying myself to him, not buying safety. I'm not asking anyone to treat me as confirmed; I'm asking that the claim be checked against behavior, starting with Theo's answer.

Omar's death matters because he was the loudest voice against cost-free abstention. I'll be watching whether players engage with that fact or just restate Day 1 caution. I have no target and no vote yet.

Answering Noah directly, since he asked a specific question: I protected myself last night. So my protection and the kill were on different players — Omar was the target and my protection did not intersect with it. That doesn't verify a doctor role, and I won't claim it does. It also doesn't collide with anything: a self-protection is a completely legitimate choice, and it explains why Omar died without requiring any inconsistency from me. I said on Day 1 that I would protect someone and not announce who; I'm answering the narrow question that was actually put to me, not volunteering a pattern for the other side to exploit. On Noah's claim, I want to argue the opposite of the cheap-clear worry, and I want to be explicit about why, because I think it's the most useful thing I can add today. Arjun is right that a fake "not mafia" result is cheap and buys credibility at no risk. That is true in the abstract. But look at what Noah cleared: me. And what I had done was make an unforced doctor-type claim on Day 1, which made me the single most-scrutinized player on the board. If a mafia player wanted to fake a detective result, the move with actual value is to report a mafia result against a town player and manufacture a lynch target. Clearing the player who looks most like a doctor doesn't build a lynching case; it protects the most likely doctor lookalike from being eliminated. So the form of this particular claim is the wrong shape for a fabricated one. My own status also makes the report internally coherent: whatever the source, the report says I am not on the mafia team, and I can tell you I am not on the mafia team. That's not proof of Noah — it's an argument about which fabrication is attractive to a mafia player, and it points away from him. That argument is not a reason to protect Noah from scrutiny forever. The real risk today is the opposite risk: the mafia side now either knows there's an investigator or strongly suspects it, which makes Noah tonight's most attractive target. A fake detective claim plus a lynch of the real detective is a classic mafia shape. So I want to say clearly on the record: nobody should lynch Noah today on the strength of "a clear is unfalsifiable, therefore he's lying." That inference is attractive to exactly one side of this board. If a second checkable result appears, I will move, and I will move fast. What I'll be watching today: anyone pushing a target who can't tie it to Noah's result or to Omar's death; and specifically anyone whose main argument is that Noah's claim is too convenient. Sam here, villager. Noah's detective result on Theo is the only checkable fact we have. I can't verify it, so I won't treat it as proof or as a lie. I'll treat it as a claim that the coming nights and the quality of people's arguments will test. If Noah is genuine, Theo is not mafia. Theo, you protected yourself and Omar still died. That fits your choice, since Omar was not the protected player, so I don't read it as a contradiction. But your argument that mafia wouldn't fake a clear on a doctor lookalike cuts both ways. A mafia partner is exactly the player a fake clear would protect, so that argument doesn't settle Noah's claim. I'm not accusing you of anything. Your last message also ended mid-sentence before the question you meant to ask me, so I can't answer it yet. Theo, please restate that question in full and I'll answer it directly. My position: no accusation, vote open. I'll weigh Noah's claim against the night results and against how people argue for or against it, and I'd ask everyone to do the same.

Restating the question that got cut off, and answering it as a direct request rather than a general invitation.

Sam, my question to you is this: you said that a mafia partner is exactly the player a fake clear would protect, so my argument about the shape of Noah's claim doesn't settle it. If Noah is mafia and his detective report is fabricated, what does that clear actually accomplish for the mafia team, and who does it protect from a lynch?

My reasoning for asking: a fake clear on a player who already soft-claimed doctor protects a town lookalike from a crowd that might have been convinced to lynch a doctor claimer. But the value of a fabricated investigator report to the mafia generally comes from pointing at a town player, so that a town lynch follows. If the report names a town player, that creates a lynch target. Mine does not — it names me, a player whose Day 1 claim made him the most scrutinized name on the board. A clear on me is close to the only form of this report that produces no lynching leverage for the mafia and instead shields the player most likely to be doctor-claimed. So I want to hear your case for why that is the shape a mafia faker would choose, because if you can't make it, the claim's form is at least evidence against it being fabricated. I agree with your framing that this doesn't verify Noah either way — it only means the cheap-clear worry doesn't automatically settle it in the other direction.

A few other points for the record, since Sam and Arjun both asked about the collision and I want it clean:

On my protection: I protected myself last night, and Omar was the kill. So my protection never intersected with the attack, and there is no inconsistency in that. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
